name: Sara Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and your answers are confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sara, 27, and I have a master’s degree in music. I lead the cello desks in a city orchestra, record short pieces for theatre and teach advanced pupils. The best hour is when the section breathes together; the worst is negotiating rights after a producer has already used our take.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sort of pay and room to move do you have now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The lead chair and recordings pay better than most music jobs, and I have about nine months of expenses saved. I live on my own and there are plenty of ensembles and schools nearby, though each post has an audition. I do not use AI tools; I have seen poor transcriptions make a simple rehearsal harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the section that the fuss has settled and we can get on with rehearsing. A calendar can be tidy without a machine listening for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and pay feel sound, though rights disputes still waste time. If little changes, I would rather bargain over the music we already record than chase every new program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the orchestra chair, my six advanced pupils and the theatre dates. This year and through the first year I'd put a fixed part of each recording fee into the savings account and ask for written reuse terms before a new session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work in this picture. Nine months of savings means a cancelled recording is a nuisance, not a rent emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those nine months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the cushion alone unless a contract ends; I built it for a real gap. I won't buy expensive gear merely because a forecast sounds exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep AI out even for routine notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong note in a printed part costs the whole section rehearsal time. I know my pencil marks, and I have no reason to hand pupils' work to a system I do not understand.

say: I would keep the **cello section** rehearsing and leave routine scheduling in the background.
I would say the **AI fuss** has settled in this picture.
think: My **lead-chair pay** and nine-month cushion make ordinary cancellations manageable.
I still want clear **recording rights** for theatre sessions.
do: Keep the **orchestra chair**, six pupils and theatre dates through the first year.
Save a fixed share of each **recording fee** this year.
Request written **reuse terms** before new sessions.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent despite occasional cancelled recordings.
S0.quote: Nine months of savings means a cancelled recording is a nuisance, not a rent emergency.
fieldNote: High pay, many nearby jobs and **nine months saved** support her calm without requiring new technology.
She sees **rights disputes** as a present problem even when AI mostly plateaus.

steps.text: Keep orchestra chair, six pupils and theatre dates
Save fixed share of each paid theatre recording fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say booking software is the least of it: the theatre may buy generated cues instead of paying players. I'd ask our musicians' union to defend minimum recording fees and consent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theatre sessions are a useful part of my income, and they could shrink without the orchestra chair disappearing. My savings soften that, but I would resent being told a copied cello line is the same as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd review the theatre contract and ask the union for a recording-rights meeting. In the first year, if session fees fall, I'd add two advanced pupils only if my timetable allows, and audition for an open orchestra chair before accepting a poor replacement fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing theatre fees, not desperate. Several ensembles are nearby, but every audition costs preparation time and there is no promise of winning one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which contract would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the clause about reusing the whole take, not just the fee for the day. A producer could save money twice if our playing becomes training material without permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a tool if the orchestra requested it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a demonstration and a written rule protecting pupils' files before touching a school tool. Until it is proven, I would keep my own lesson notes on paper.

say: I would warn that generated **theatre cues** may replace paid players.
I would ask the **musicians’ union** for minimum fees and recording consent.
think: Theatre sessions may shrink while my **orchestra chair** remains.
Nearby **auditions** are options, but they take time and offer no guarantee.
do: Review the **theatre contract** and ask the union for a rights meeting now.
Add two **advanced pupils** if fees fall and my timetable permits.
Audition for an open **chair** before accepting a poor replacement fee.
feel: I feel **anxious** about theatre income, despite savings and nearby auditions.
S1.quote: Several ensembles are nearby, but every audition costs preparation time and there is no promise of winning one.
fieldNote: She locates the first **income loss** in theatre sessions rather than the orchestra chair.
Her **union request** targets reuse as well as pay; extra pupils depend on timetable space.

steps.text: Ask musicians’ union for theatre recording-rights meeting now
Add two advanced pupils if fees fall and timetable permits
Audition for open orchestra chair before taking a poor replacement fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that thinking AGI in 2028 could replace arranging and lesson materials before capable robots arrive around 2031. We should negotiate what happens to our recorded work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid theatre cues might go in two years, and some families may buy automated coaching. I would still have a live chair for a while, but my income could fall more than a comfortable account suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd ask the union to settle a consent clause and keep my nine-month cushion intact. In the first year after 2028, if theatre calls stop, I'd cut my studio rental day, seek paid pupils at the music school if a room and places are offered, and audition for a posted orchestra vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a part of the work I earned slowly. I have time and local options, but neither makes a vanished session fee reappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2028 before a robot can play cello?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cello chair still needs hands until roughly 2031 in this picture. The three years before robot cellists arrive protect my chair, but not my theatre recording fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the cushion would you risk on a new plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend the savings on my own studio without signed pupils. If the school offers a room and families actually book, I could pay for a term; otherwise I would protect the cushion.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from capable robots around 2031.
I would ask the orchestra to secure **recording consent** now.
think: Paid **theatre cues** and some teaching income could fall quickly.
My savings buy time but cannot keep **session fees** flowing.
do: Seek a **union consent clause** before 2028 while protecting my savings cushion.
Cut the **studio rental day** if theatre calls stop after 2028.
Replace lost fees through **school pupils** if a room opens, or audition for a posted chair after 2028.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost recording fees despite savings and nearby options.
S2.quote: The three years before robot cellists arrive protect my chair, but not my theatre recording fees.
fieldNote: Her **thinking work** could shrink in 2028 while the live cello chair lasts closer to 2031.
She refuses to **rent studio space** without signed pupils, even with nine months saved.

steps.text: Ask musicians’ union to settle recording consent before 2028
Cut studio rental day if theatre calls stop after 2028
Seek paid school pupils after 2028 theatre loss if room and places offered
Audition for posted orchestra vacancies in first year after 2028 if theatre calls stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union we have until 2031 to secure consent, rates and a way to challenge misuse. Robots that can play follow around 2034, so we should protect the live chair too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to decide whether teaching can replace theatre sessions. I am not eager to change instruments, software or city when a proper contract may keep this job viable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the school about a regular advanced-cello class if it can guarantee a room and paid places. Before 2031 I'd seek a union recording agreement; in the first year after AGI, I'd keep the orchestra chair if it remains paid and offer the class only if enough pupils enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about future fees, but I can make a careful case instead of a leap. A signed class list matters more to me than a clever prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the union agenda?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put recording consent, reuse pay and a clear complaint route on the agenda. A union agreement is useful only if a player can enforce it after the recording leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer warning make you change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would audition elsewhere only if this orchestra cuts the paid chair or refuses basic recording terms. There are posts nearby, but I won't leave a good section merely to show I am adaptable.

say: I would seek **union consent** and rates before thinking AGI arrives in 2031.
I would prepare the **live chair** for robots arriving around 2034.
think: Five years could show whether **advanced teaching** replaces theatre fees.
A sound contract may let me stay with my **current section**.
do: Ask the school for a **regular class** only if it guarantees a room and paid places.
Keep the **paid chair** after 2031; audition elsewhere only if it is cut or basic recording terms are refused.
feel: I feel **anxious** about future fees, preferring signed class lists over speculative moves.
S3.quote: A signed class list matters more to me than a clever prediction.
fieldNote: She treats **school teaching** as conditional on a room, paid places and enough enrolment.
Her **union agenda** includes a complaint route so consent and reuse terms can be enforced.

steps.text: Ask school for advanced class if room and paid places are guaranteed
Seek enforceable recording agreement through union before 2031
Keep orchestra chair in first year after 2031 if it remains paid
Audition elsewhere if paid chair is cut or basic recording terms refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players that they have a decade to build strong ears, teaching ties and fair contracts. Thinking AGI in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039 are separate dates, not today's dismissal notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might lose some recording work, and robot players could challenge live seats at about 40. I cannot promise a cello chair forever, but nine months of savings and several local schools give me choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the orchestra and six pupils this year, and add to savings from each paid theatre date. Over the decade I'd build a school class only if it offers a room and paid places; in the first year after 2036 I'd keep teaching and audition for open chairs if the orchestra reduces mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm with time to plan and money set aside. My own nine-month cushion does not cover the colleague beside me. I would still fight for musicians' rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the decade do for your teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would let me teach an extra level of students gradually, if the school actually has room. I will not count a class as income until the names and fees are on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date alter your retirement thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement at forty is not my plan, even if robots can play. I would aim for paid teaching and a live chair as long as listeners and schools still want them.

say: I would tell younger players to build **teaching ties** and fair contracts.
I would keep **2036 AGI** distinct from capable robots around 2039.
think: I cannot guarantee a **cello chair** forever, even with strong savings.
Several **local schools** give me possible routes if recording work declines.
do: Keep the **orchestra chair** and six pupils this year, saving from each paid theatre date.
Build a **school class** only if it offers a room and paid places.
Audition for open **chairs** after 2036 if the orchestra reduces my paid position.
feel: I feel fairly **calm**, while caring about colleagues with less savings.
S4.quote: My own nine-month cushion does not cover the colleague beside me.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to AI** persists; she uses the long horizon for contracts and teaching, not tools.
She rejects **early retirement** and will audition only if her paid chair shrinks.

steps.text: Keep orchestra chair and six advanced pupils this year
Save part of each paid theatre session fee
Build school class only if room and paid places are offered
Audition for open chairs in first year after 2036 if orchestra reduces paid position

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the theatre fees could go before we get useful recording protections. An enforceable union clause and access to a paid teaching room would help. My savings give me time, but they cannot force a producer to honour a recording agreement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose work gets called safe when people say musicians can just play live. A cello section has a stage and a rent bill, and the theatre recording often joins the two.

headlineQuote: A cello section has a stage and a rent bill, and the theatre recording often joins the two.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old cellist** with a master’s degree, leading an orchestra section, teaching advanced pupils and recording theatre parts.
Higher pay, **nine months saved** and many nearby posts give her room to respond to lost session work.
She **never uses AI** and prefers contracts, auditions and proven teaching places to new software.
The faster scenarios expose **theatre fees** before robot players arrive, while union consent and paid school space shape her plans.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** will remove theatre fees before the union secures enforceable recording rights.
whatWouldHelp: An enforceable **union clause** would protect consent and reuse payments.
A **paid teaching room** would let her take school pupils without risking her savings.
